Thank you for your issue! We have categorized it as a feature request, and it has been added to our backlog. In doing so, **we are not committing to implementing this feature at this time**, but, we will consider it for future releases based on community feedback and our own product roadmap. 

Unless you see the https://github.com/cli/cli/labels/help%20wanted label, we are not currently looking for external contributions for this feature.

**If you come across this issue and would like to see it implemented, please add a thumbs up!** This will help us prioritize the feature. Please only comment if you have additional information or viewpoints to contribute.

body:
Hi @mara004! 👋

I'll leave the answer to folks who are well-versed in this domain, @bdehamer and @ejahnGithub, but as a general restriction `gh` requires the user to be logged in before calling any command that involves communicating with the API. For example, you cannot run `gh issue list --repo cli/cli` without being logged in, although the repo is public.

One important reason for this restriction, among others, is that `gh` needs to provide a deterministic experience. Some API endpoints behave differently when they're invoked without a token. They don't necessarily return an `HTTP 40x`, but rather a refined version of the underlying data. In such cases the experience would be confusing to the user.

Hi @babakks and thanks for the feedback.

I can see this is difficult with gh as it is usually tied to a GitHub account.

But the problem for us as user of GitHub attestations remains: attestation verification depending on authentication and a GitHub account is fundamentally problematic and reduces the surface where automatic verification can be meaningfully used.

If this doesn't fit in gh itself, then we'd need an alternative, documented way to programmatically verify a GitHub attestation without token / account. Similar e.g. to SLSA provenance which is managed as an artifact and can be verified with `slsa-verifier` without additional requirements that complicate the process.

Hi @mara004. There's a couple of things `gh attestation verify` does:

- It fetches the Sigstore bundle from GitHub's attestation API (this is usually what requires authentication)
- It ensures it has up-to-date verification information from GitHub artifact attestations
- It [performs the verification](https://blog.sigstore.dev/cosign-verify-end-user/) of the Sigstore bundle by providing information about the expected Sigstore instance, the identity provider (GitHub Actions), and what identities from that provider to trust (in your case this could be something like "any repositories owned by `https://github.com/mara004`")

There's a lot of things to think about in this process, and it's easy to miss a step or be confused about what information to provide where, which is why we strongly recommend people use `gh attestation verify` - it puts a very user-friendly interface on this complex process.

However. Since GitHub artifact attestations is based on the specifications from the Sigstore ecosystem, it is compatible with other Sigstore tooling. See for example the ["GitHub Artifact Attestations" section of a Sigstore blog post](https://blog.sigstore.dev/cosign-verify-bundles/) for details on how to verify GitHub artifact attestations with Sigstore's cosign CLI. Again, I would not recommend this approach, but it is possible to do so.

It would also be possible to verify this content with https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore-python, although I'm not sure anyone has written a guide to do so.

@steiza I've read about cosign in the [verification bootstrapping instructions](https://github.com/cli/cli?tab=readme-ov-file#verification-of-binaries) in this repo, but what's not so obvious to me is how to *programmatically* obtain the attestation bundle that corresponds to the (or multiple) release artifact(s), without again resorting to `gh attestation {download, trusted-root}` commands which assumably also require a token.

> There's a lot of things to think about in this process, and it's easy to miss a step or be confused about what information to provide where, which is why we strongly recommend people use `gh attestation verify` - it puts a very user-friendly interface on this complex process.

It may be user-friendly for authenticated end users, yes, but it isn't really suitable for use in an automated pipeline that should be able to run anywhere without an account.
So it would be great to have a tool similar to `gh attestation verify` that handles the complex process but does not require authentication.

Ah, okay, I think I understand the difference in perspective now.

`gh attestation verify` actually **does not** require GitHub authentication **when** you supply the bundle. This is because the bundle download (`gh attestation download`) uses GitHub REST APIs. All GitHub REST APIs, even for public repositories, are heavily rate-limited for unauthenticated users; this has nothing to do with artifact attestations, but instead because of abuse across the entire GitHub platform 😞 

So if you want to download the bundles (when authenticated) and store them and distribute them yourself, I think you could use `gh attestation verify` without authenticating. But if you want GitHub to store the bundles for you, you will need to be authenticated - regardless of if you're using `gh` or if you wrote your own code to call the [REST API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/users/attestations?apiVersion=2022-11-28&versionId=free-pro-team%40latest&category=orgs&subcategory=attestations) directly.

I was just about to post this at the same time @steiza's comment arrived:

-----

I think I found out how to do it after all:
```bash
curl -L https://api.github.com/repos/$OWNER/$REPO/attestations/sha256:$HASH > attestation-info.json
```
Extract `["attestations"][0]["bundle"]` from the JSON and save it to a new file.
Then use `gh`'s offline verification mode (partially, anyway):
```bash
gh at verify $ARTIFACT.tgz -R $OWNER/$REPO -b bundle.json
```
This works without authentication (tested in a plain docker container), and the attestation bundle can be used for any artifact in the release in question.

> All GitHub REST APIs, even for public repositories, are heavily rate-limited for unauthenticated users; this has nothing to do with artifact attestations, but instead because of abuse across the entire GitHub platform 😞

> But if you want GitHub to store the bundles for you, you will need to be authenticated - regardless of if you're using gh or if you wrote your own code to call the [REST API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/users/attestations?apiVersion=2022-11-28&versionId=free-pro-team%40latest&category=orgs&subcategory=attestations) directly.

Hmm, as you can see the above REST call seems to work without authentication.
(BTW, I tried `https://api.github.com/users/$USER/attestations/bulk-list` first which returned an error insisting on authentication)

I would just give it a try and see how it goes with the rate limit.
FWIW I've already used the REST API (and artifact downloads) unauthenticated in the past and so far haven't had issues with the limits...

Okay, rate limits are indeed a potential issue with Github Actions runners – I think because they may have been exhausted by previous users of that runner.
See e.g. https://github.com/pypdfium2-team/pypdfium2/actions/runs/18244860456/job/51951460770 for a job that failed.

See https://github.com/pypdfium2-team/pypdfium2/blob/683c8cec7fb7348b65c1d196fdf9471f656239b8/setupsrc/pypdfium2_setup/_verify.py#L63-L117 for a hardened version of the above code.

In a re-run verification still fails on a subset of jobs, but does not fail our task as a whole:
https://github.com/pypdfium2-team/pypdfium2/actions/runs/18245212542/job/51952240899#step:4:250

@steiza 

FYI, your statement:

> However. Since GitHub artifact attestations is based on the specifications from the Sigstore ecosystem, it is compatible with other Sigstore tooling. See for example the ["GitHub Artifact Attestations" section of a Sigstore blog post](https://blog.sigstore.dev/cosign-verify-bundles/) for details on how to verify GitHub artifact attestations with Sigstore's cosign CLI. Again, I would not recommend this approach, but it is possible to do so.

Is misleading because that blog post states in Step 2 to `gh attestation download...` which leads us straight back to the authentication required trap.

The simple truth is that:

1. End-users should not be required to register a github account to verify assets published by developers; and
2. Sysadmins who want to integrate asset downloads into provisioning scripts should not have to embed github credentials into their scripts

The present situation is nuts.  It simply forces everybody back to the 90's and just verifying the checksum file assets published by the developers.  Which although it provides integrity does not do anything for verifying authenticity.

@udf2457 Consider adding the attestation as a release artifact, or if you don't have control over the project in question, ask its maintainers to do so. This bypasses the need for a token, and is the workaround we finally ended up with. LLVM also do this.

That said, I agree the present state is annoying and deserves improvement from the GH side. (`gh attestation verify` being unable to verify multiple files at once is also vexing.)

@mara004 so in your repo release assets its the [pypdfium2-attestation.json](https://github.com/pypdfium2-team/pypdfium2/releases/download/5.9.0/pypdfium2-attestation.json), not [Release attestation (json)](https://github.com/pypdfium2-team/pypdfium2/attestations/29421912/download) correct ?

In my particular scenario its 99% other maintainers, and from experience trying to get them to make changes to their release workflow as a random outsider tends to be a painful experience.

> @mara004 so in your repo release assets its the [pypdfium2-attestation.json](https://github.com/pypdfium2-team/pypdfium2/releases/download/5.9.0/pypdfium2-attestation.json), not [Release attestation (json)](https://github.com/pypdfium2-team/pypdfium2/attestations/29421912/download) correct ?

Yes. "Release attestation (json)" is something GH adds automatically, I think, if immutable releases are enabled.
It is not actually a provenance attestation, and in effect more like a checksum, as far as I understand.

> In my particular scenario its 99% other maintainers, and from experience trying to get them to make changes to their release workflow as a random outsider tends to be a painful experience.

I see the trouble... Yet, other maintainers might also see the token requirement as a problem, so it may be at least worth trying to ask or propose PRs.

> In my particular scenario its 99% other maintainers, and from experience trying to get them to make changes to their release workflow as a random outsider tends to be a painful experience.

OK, given how https://github.com/go-acme/lego/issues/2167 turned, I quite agree you were right...

@mara004 Yeah, I really appreciate your efforts there.  ❤️ 

I don't know what `gh attestation trusted-root` does, but given it does not return immediately I'm guessing it downloads stuff in the background.  So I'm not sure why Github cannot just grant a general exception to the authentication requirement for _any_ `gh attestation` command.
